extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers preparing grant applications (NIH, ERC) / scientists interested in how grant review works
extracted.subtask_description: Explains how the NIH two-stage peer-review process works, what reviewers score and write, empirical findings about reviewer agreement and randomness, plus practical advice for applicants (minimise weaknesses, resubmit addressing critiques). Also contrasts ERC evaluation priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH two-stage review process
rubrics_metrics.description: The NIH uses a two-stage review process: (1) between two and five reviewers individually evaluate each grant application, rate them using NIH’s nine-point scale, and record application strengths and weaknesses; (2) members of NIH advisory councils use the resulting priority score and the written critiques to make funding recommendations to the Director of the NIH institute or centre that awards the funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcript explanation: stage one = individual reviews and study section meeting discussion of the top half of applications, producing a final rating averaged into a priority score; stage two = advisory councils consider priority score and critiques to recommend funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH nine-point scoring and written critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers rate applications on NIH’s nine-point scale (1 = exceptional to 9 = poor) and record perceived strengths and weaknesses in written critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The numeric score is tied to the written review: within an individual reviewer, 'the more weaknesses they identified in the proposal, the lower the score awarded.' Applicants should be aware that reviewers document both scores and strengths/weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study section discussion and triage (top-half discussion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study section meetings only discuss the top half of applications based on preliminary ratings; those discussed receive collective final ratings that are averaged into a priority score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of triage, only the top ~50% of applications get discussed; applications below that threshold are effectively excluded from meeting-based reconsideration, which affects chances for funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer agreement / calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of agreement between different reviewers is low: reviewers may be internally consistent (their number of weaknesses predicts their own scores) but different reviewers have different calibrations of what constitutes a good or bad score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pier’s study found 'no agreement between different individual reviewers in the score that they assigned' and that each reviewer had a different idea of what a weakness is and what score that implied — implying calibration among reviewers is a key factor in reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel consensus vs. between-panel variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion within a panel tends to narrow score ranges (consensus building), but different panels evaluating the same applications can diverge after discussion, increasing between-panel variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the recreated panels, 'the range of scores does get smaller after discussions' within a panel, but 'the agreement between different panels actually got wider after discussion' — suggesting meetings may not improve cross-panel reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomness / luck above a quality threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications that clear the initial quality threshold (i.e., among the top ~50%), outcomes appear to contain a large random component — luck plays a large role in whether competitive applications are funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pier: 'Above a certain quality threshold... it’s essentially a random process' and the study suggests substantial randomness in who does and does not get funding among competitive proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of triage on meritorious but un-discussed applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Because donations in the study were all previously funded applications, the analysis applies to discussed applications; applications triaged out (not discussed) may nevertheless have merits and could have fared differently with other panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: 'the applications that get discussed... have already gone through triage' so some good proposals may be 'weeded out' before meeting discussion; assignment to a different panel could alter whether an application is discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal to use a modified lottery
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed alternative is a 'modified lottery system': initial expert screening to weed out clearly problematic proposals (feasibility, budget, blatant issues), then random selection among those that pass the screen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: if selection is effectively random above a quality threshold, a lottery could save money and time spent convening many reviewers and meetings; still requires an initial expert screen to remove infeasible proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical applicant advice — minimise weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Weaknesses are much more predictive of the score reviewers will assign than strengths, so applicants should minimise as many weaknesses as possible in their proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pier’s explicit advice: focus on reducing weaknesses in the submission; when rejected, resubmit and be responsive to reviewer critiques because responsiveness over resubmissions 'can play a strong role in conveying to reviewers improvement over time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical applicant advice — resilience and responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should not take rejection personally; respond constructively to critiques, revise and resubmit, and persist, since resubmission that addresses reviewer feedback can improve outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pier: 'there is something to be said for... resubmitting that application and doing everything you can to address the reviewers’ critiques and feedback' — tenacity matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: ERC evaluation focus: project over host institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The ERC evaluation emphasizes the project itself rather than the applicant’s host institution; host institution is not part of evaluation although applicants must describe needed resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jean‑Pierre Bourguignon: 'the institution which is your host institution is not part of the evaluation... the key for the evaluation is the project.' Applicants should show what resources are needed and describe them, but selection is project-focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: ERC eligibility categories and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC grants have three categories: Starting Grants (2–7 years post-PhD), Consolidator Grants (7–12 years), and Advanced Grants (no time condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These eligibility windows determine which career-stage calls applicants may apply to; ERC allocates a large fraction of budget to younger researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: ERC priority: high-risk, ambitious research and researcher independence
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC encourages ambitious, high-risk research and early independence: panels are urged to take risks and the ERC seeks to fund ambitious projects, placing researchers 'in the driver’s seat.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourguignon notes the ERC funds projects considered 'too risky' by other national agencies and expects panels to accept risk; typical ERC success rate noted (~13%) underscores competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: ERC practical rules: portability and residence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC grants offer portability (researcher may change host institution) and require grantees to spend at least 50% of their time in Europe, while being open to applicants from any country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portability empowers researchers to change host institutions; the '50% time in Europe' rule is a funding-condition constraint applicants must meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity and outreach in ERC selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The ERC actively monitors and addresses gender and regional imbalances (e.g., increasing female applicant share, supporting underrepresented regions/EU13) as part of its selection ecosystem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourguignon describes targeted efforts (encouraging applications, regional support schemes, training opportunities) intended to raise application rates and success for underrepresented groups and regions.
